opus-5.5.text:
Fusion is one of the areas I'm most excited about, because it's a problem where traditional simulation becomes the bottleneck. To design a reactor, whether a tokamak or a stellarator, you need to understand how the plasma behaves under extreme conditions. That means solving very complex physics: magnetohydrodynamics, turbulence, transport, all coupled across many scales in space and time. Running these simulations with conventional numerical solvers can take days or weeks for a single configuration, which makes it nearly impossible to explore the design space properly.

Stellarators are especially interesting and especially hard. Unlike tokamaks, which are roughly axisymmetric, stellarators have these twisted three-dimensional magnetic coil geometries. That gives you advantages, like better steady-state operation and fewer disruptions, but the design space is enormous. You're optimizing the shape of the coils and the magnetic field in full 3D, and every candidate needs expensive physics evaluation.

Our approach is built around neural operators. The key idea is that instead of learning a mapping between fixed-size vectors, like a standard neural network, we learn mappings between function spaces. A neural operator learns the solution operator of the underlying partial differential equations. So it isn't tied to a particular mesh or resolution. You can train on data at one resolution and evaluate at another, which matters a lot when your training data comes from simulations at different fidelities.

Once you have a neural operator trained as a surrogate for the plasma dynamics, you can evaluate it thousands, sometimes up to a million, times faster than the traditional solver. That changes what's possible. Instead of carefully hand-picking a few designs to simulate, you can do large-scale design optimization: sweep over coil geometries, magnetic configurations, and operating parameters, and use gradient-based optimization because the operator is differentiable end to end.

We've done work on predicting plasma evolution, for example forecasting how the plasma state evolves in a reactor from camera or sensor data, which is important for control. You want to anticipate instabilities before they happen and adjust in real time. With classical solvers you simply can't run fast enough for real-time control. With neural operators, you can.

Another important piece is making these models physics-informed. We don't want a black box that fits data and then produces unphysical results when you push it outside the training distribution. So we incorporate the PDE constraints directly into training, sometimes alongside observational or simulation data. That gives you better generalization and much more data efficiency, which matters because high-fidelity fusion data is scarce and expensive.

The bigger vision is that AI doesn't replace the physics; it accelerates it. You still need the domain knowledge from plasma physicists and the high-fidelity simulations as ground truth. But neural operators let you explore far more of the design space, find promising candidates much faster, and then validate the best ones with the expensive solvers or experiments. For something like stellarators, where the geometry is so complex and intuition only goes so far, that kind of fast, broad exploration could really shorten the path to practical fusion energy.

r001.rationale: The response describes using neural operators to optimize and evaluate fusion designs, but does not identify a digital twin as the goal.

r002.rationale: It mentions both tokamaks and stellarators, but its exploration is described mainly as optimizing stellarator configurations; it does not clearly advocate exploring competing fusion approaches without choosing a winner in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about fusion is that it's fundamentally a design and control problem, and the bottleneck has always been simulation. If you want to understand what the plasma is going to do inside a tokamak or a stellarator, you're solving these very hard coupled PDEs, magnetohydrodynamics, kinetic effects, turbulence across many scales, and a single high-fidelity run can take days or weeks on a supercomputer. That means in practice you only get to evaluate a handful of designs. You pick a geometry, you run it, you look at the results, and you iterate very slowly.

What we've been doing is replacing those expensive solvers with neural operators. The key idea with something like the Fourier neural operator is that instead of learning a function from inputs to outputs at a fixed grid, you learn a mapping between function spaces. So you train on simulation data, and then the model can predict the plasma evolution for a new geometry or a new set of coil currents orders of magnitude faster, thousands of times faster in many cases, and it's resolution-invariant, so you can query it at resolutions you didn't train on. Once you have that, the whole workflow changes. You're no longer evaluating ten designs, you're evaluating millions, and you can do gradient-based optimization directly through the surrogate.

Stellarators are where this gets really interesting. Tokamaks are axisymmetric, so the geometry is relatively constrained. A stellarator gets its confinement from the three-dimensional shaping of the coils, which means the design space is enormous. There are hundreds or thousands of parameters describing the coil shapes, and the physics is very sensitive to them. That has historically been the big disadvantage of stellarators, they're incredibly hard to design and build. But it's exactly the kind of problem where a fast differentiable surrogate is a huge win, because you can actually search that space. You can ask: what shaping gives me good confinement, low turbulent transport, and coils that are actually manufacturable, all at the same time.

The other piece is control. Fusion plasmas are unstable, you have disruptions, tearing modes, things that happen on millisecond timescales. We've done work on learning predictors for those instabilities and then using reinforcement learning or model-based control to steer the plasma away from them in real time. You can't do that with a traditional simulator in the loop because it's far too slow. So the same neural operator that helps you design the machine also lets you run it.

I'd add one caveat, which is that these models are only as good as the data and the physics you build in. So we spend a lot of effort on making sure they respect conservation laws, that they're calibrated with uncertainty, and that we validate against real experimental data from devices like DIII-D or Wendelstein 7-X. The goal isn't to replace the physicists, it's to give them a tool where the iteration loop goes from months to minutes, and that's what I think actually accelerates the path to a working reactor.

r001.rationale: The response describes neural operators as fast surrogates for evaluating and optimizing fusion designs, but it does not identify a digital twin as the setting or goal.

r002.rationale: It describes searching many designs, especially stellarator coil configurations, but does not advocate exploring competing fusion approaches without choosing a winner in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting opportunity is to use AI to make the design process much faster. With fusion, you’re dealing with very complex plasma dynamics, and running a high-fidelity simulation for every possible design is expensive. If we can learn a surrogate for those simulations, we can explore a much broader range of designs and then validate the most promising ones with the physics solver.

Stellarators are a particularly interesting example because their magnetic geometry is so intricate. The question is: can we optimize that geometry to get good plasma confinement while also respecting engineering constraints, like whether the coils can actually be built? You want to bring those constraints into the optimization from the beginning.

And this is where neural operators offer an exciting approach: learning mappings between functions so we can predict physical fields across different configurations. The goal is to combine that speed with physics-based validation and ultimately experiments, creating a feedback loop that helps us discover better designs.

r001.rationale: The response describes speeding up design exploration with surrogate simulations, but does not identify a digital twin as the goal.

r002.rationale: It proposes exploring a broader range of designs, but does not clearly advocate comparing competing fusion approaches without choosing a winner in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of this as an inverse design problem. You start with the properties you want—stable plasma confinement, for instance—and ask what geometry and operating conditions could produce them. With stellarators, the magnetic geometry is very complex, so exploring that design space with traditional simulations can be expensive.

AI can help by learning a surrogate for those simulations, allowing us to evaluate candidate designs much faster. Then we can put that model inside an optimization loop to search for promising configurations. The key is to include physical and engineering constraints, and to validate those candidates with high-fidelity simulations and, ultimately, experiments.

What’s exciting is the possibility of exploring a much broader range of designs. But we also need to know when the model is uncertain, so we can run additional simulations where they will teach us the most.

r001.rationale: The response describes inverse design and faster simulation for stellarator configurations, but does not identify designing fusion systems within a digital twin as the goal.

r002.rationale: It supports exploring a broader range of designs, but does not clearly describe comparing competing fusion approaches without choosing a winner in advance.
